Frostpunk really makes you feel inadequate.

Morality in this game is used as a punishment for poor leadership. If you're not able to provide for your people, then you'll have to make bad decisions to keep them alive. Like employing children in mines or beating disobedient people to silence them. In my first playthrough, I had to deliberately let dozens of people die to save hundreds. 

Rather than simply posing morality as a role-playing element (be good or be evil), this game puts you in the shoes of a leader who is unable to 'do the right thing' because you lack the expertise to keep people alive while maintaining your humanity. You begin to understand religion as a tool to keep people happy. You use tyrannical rule to keep people from spreading discontent. You let people fight each other in pits to keep them entertained. Anything to keep people through another day.

Your ability to make higher moral choices is dependent on your ability to manage resources. Through my playthroughs I made plenty of poor moral choices, but only because I believed I had to. I felt genuine remorse because I knew these choices were a consequence of my poor management. It wasn't a matter of changing my outlook or adopting better morals, but a matter of becoming a better manager. It's a problem real leaders face, and this game provides a thoughtful, philosophical light on what it means to lead people through dire situations, and the choices one is forced to make to maintain order.

This game is incredible. I remember looking at it for a while and thinking it didn't seem like anything special. You're in a frozen wasteland and you build a circular city around a generator. That's basically the gist of it. However, what starts as a resource-balancing act becomes complicated by difficult choices with no clear-cut answers, and storylines that don't always play out how you would expect. The game doesn't highlight the "good" or "evil" option, and in fact, the morally bad option is sometimes your best chance at survival.

I started my first playthrough as a good guy, honestly. My religious community was doing great, and I was doing my best to bring in survivors from the wasteland. I wanted to be the good guy and help everyone. Before I knew it, my city was extremely overpopulated and headed toward starvation. People were threatening to riot. Hope was low, and discontent was high. The people were demanding warm housing, but I knew a massive storm was just days away. Hundreds would freeze and die.

So I lied through my teeth and told them I would totally house every last person, raising their hope and quelling their anger. When the storm hit, lots of those angry people ended up dead. One less mouth to feed. This completely tanked my hope and I was nearly exiled into the white oblivion, but I simply declared sovereign law and used brute force to beat everyone into submission. My zealots set up an executioner's block and roasted infidels alive. It was horrifying. At least we didn't have to start cannibalizing all the slave-children who died from hypothermia in the mines.

The storm passed, and the city survived. I had won... but at what cost?

I thought this was going to be a depressing hard choices simulator, which kept me away for a long time. When I finally gave it a shot I was surprised at how much it's about endurance, hope, and human ingenuity. It's definitely not easy, but you can not just survive but thrive. (It's kind of a shame that once you thrive the game basically plays itself, but you can consider that a reward.)

Can you imagine... living in a society where people are willing to work together to do what is necessary to survive a world-threatening climate disaster?

Good stuff first. It's a fantastic city builder, and it includes survival mechanics so you feel like you're playing tug-of-war with the arctic weather, racing to complete one more milestone before things get colder so you can survive another day. The atmosphere (Apocalyptic steampunk!) is wonderful, and the game's mechanics work incredibly well. The building system even manages to soothe my city-building perfectionism because it will slightly adjust building sizes to make sure you're using every available inch with no ugly gaps between buildings. The scenarios are challenging, the stories are compelling, there's lots of replay value, and you can easily put a hundred hours into this game. Wonderful devs too, who have released a [i] ton [/i] of free content and updates since the game released a year ago.

The one minor flaw to this game is that after you complete it on normal difficulty, you move to the 'hard' and 'extreme' difficulty levels. Those difficulties are completely unbalanced and you wind up needing to follow an ironclad beginning build order that takes advantage of how the game is coded to prevent your city from going into a death spiral. For instance, in the first 30 seconds of the Winterhome scenario you might need to sign a law and then build a medical tent, but if you place the med tent first and [i] then [/i] sign the law, 20 people will die. This wouldn't be so bad, but from what I've seen online, these build orders are checklists for the first 1-2 hours of a city. The game stops being fun for me when you have to spend that long with a razor-thin margin where you're not even making your own decisions of what to do next.

The good news is that the normal difficulty level is perfectly balanced, and you'll get 80ish hours of gameplay out of it. Also, with how responsive the devs have been, it's possible they may tweak the difficulty levels to make the harder difficulties more playable.

[b] tl;dr - You'll love this game and should buy it. Normal difficulty is perfect and will last you 80+ hours, but the harder difficulties are almost broken. [/b]

(Much better first time you play it, but then it loses its edge)

============

Review:

Frostpunk is a good survival/builder game, but you will quickly see all that the game has to offer.

Basically you start with a small amount of people and you have to survive. You need to build shelter against the cold (housing), and gather a few basic resources that allows you to progress. Things like coal, wood, steel and food. You need these resources for heating, building, research etc.

You build things like sawmills, hothouses and mines to get these resources. At the very beginning there's a few things scattered around that you can just gather to get you started.

You research new buildings and upgrades with Workshops - and researching requires wood and steel - these scale with tech tiers.

More advanced buildings require Steam Cores which you cannot produce yourself - these must be gathered from locations on the map and are finite - so you have to plan your "build" accordingly.

Later the weather keeps getting colder and colder and you need to have better heating technology or your people will freeze to death.

============

Audiovisually the game is very good - the graphics of the game are good and the sound-world creates immersion nicely. The game also has very good music - it fits the late 1800's survival theme very well. 

I especially like how the music "evolves" with the events. This is especially notable during the last days of the game - The music helps set the "panic" and "despair" during your first attempt at playing the game.

I really like the ending animation of the game - it shows how you expanded your city and tells you what kind of choices you did during your run - good or bad.

============

The very first time you play it is an experience worthy of a five star rating - because you have no idea what to do, what's coming or how to optimize so the survival aspect is real. Every day will be a struggle, survival is like walking on a tightrope, and it feels like you're about to lose constantly.

It is a very exciting experience in my opinion and even though I did survive (barely) on my first attempt it felt really challenging.

But after the first time, when you replay the game it just loses its edge. Because you know what to do, and how to optimize. The game will no longer be that exciting everyday struggle for survival when you have massive surplus of everything.

Yes, you can increase the difficulty to make things harder, but still you have seen the events and all and know what's coming - it's just not that exciting anymore.

So do NOT use spoilers or watch videos to make your first attempt easier - just play it!

============

Overall, I think Frostpunk is a good game. The first time is excellent, but after that it's not so great anymore. But still, replaying it with different styles can be fun. Or trying different scenarios for replayability.

I highly recommend the game despite giving it only a "good" rating - simply because of the awesome first time you will get if you do not spoil things for yourself.

But if you plan to play it only once, then you should wait for a sale. It's not worth the full price if you just want that one great and exciting run with it.

============

I both really like Frostpunk and am also really frustrated by it. The core concept and aesthetic are great. The sense of desperation you feel is genuine as difficulties mount. And seriously, when the heavy duty music kicks in, you grip your mouse fiercely. And for a good while, it's easy to be hooked. 

However, once you reach a certain point, you realize that it isn't so much a strategic resource sim as it is a puzzle. It wants you to build in a certain way, and if you don't, expect to get your ass handed to you quickly. It wants you to think you're making meaningful moral choices, but the two branches end up pretty similar, and they aren't so much *choices* as things you have to agree to in order to move ahead. 

All that said, I still put a good number of hours in because I was willing to work through the puzzle. Ultimately, I think the good outweighs the bad *IF* you're willing to accept the actual limitations of what it is. And I think this is the foundation of what could be a truly incredible game if they truly provided freedom to win on your own terms and gave you a truly developed moral/leadership system.

For me, it’s a zen garden made of steel and steam. While my actual life is a chaotic open world with no tutorial, Frostpunk lets me build a perfect circle of logic in a frozen wasteland. Is it a bit 'of the "tism'' in me to find peace in micromanaging heat maps and ration distributions while the temperature drops to -120°C? Maybe. For me, this isn't a game about suffering; it’s a game about order. In a world that feels like an unpredictable mess, Frostpunk is the one place where I can work out every problem and know exactly what’s coming. I’m the Captain, and my spreadsheets are the only thing keeping us from becoming popsicles.

Frostpunk is a city builder / survival game that lets you build and manage a colony of fortunate survivors of a frozen and desolate Earth.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
Frostpunk is very relentless; from the initial start of your central generator to a resolute habitable city along the frozen wastelands, you need to be very careful. It took me a couple of failures to finally figure out the game and what proper paths to take in order to finish the different scenarios available. The gameplay revolves around providing adequate heat and food to your colony in the form of shelter, generators, and food hunting/cooking. You also need to mine and gather the needed resources to keep things functioning like coals for generators and machines, and wood and steel for construction and research. You also need to balance and manage the disposition of your colonists. Their 'hope' and 'discontent' by providing wanted and needed amenities to avoid mass panic and revolts. You can also send expeditions to the outside world, to explore and discover new things.

The main danger of Frostpunk is the blistering cold. As the game goes on, temperature will drop bit by bit, requiring you to research and improve your colony in order to adapt to the constantly decreasing temperatures. One mistake can lead to a cascade of failures; failure to cure the sick will lead to widespread panic and therefore laborers won't be able to work efficiently, thus losing valuable resources essential to keeping the colony running like coal to fuel the generators, that in turn provide heat to your buildings and shelters.

One colony enforcement mechanic called 'Book of Laws' is a pretty interesting feature that allows you to shape your city into your liking by offering you choices and solutions on how to tackle different issues and problems, for example choosing to allow child labor or allowing them to live as normal children, all with different benefits and drawbacks. It ultimately leads to two opposing paths; Faith and Order.

Frostpunk offers four different scenarios that presents different starting conditions, challenges, and goals. All with excellent and engaging storytelling, one of the best I've seen in a strategy game. It also has an endless mode with different maps and sub-modes, however despite this, replayability goes down the drain once you have finished the four initial scenarios and 'figure' it out. It does not give a lot of freedom for the players, there is only a few viable paths to optimally play and beat the game. As a result a lot of people are requesting for more content, although it's more of a testament to how great Frostpunk is that people are wanting more, as opposed to actually lacking proper content. The four scenarios alone already offers a lot of hours of gameplay, not even counting the ones where you fail and restart all over. 

[h1]Technical Analysis[/h1]
Frostpunk absolutely nailed the depiction of a steampunk city on a freezing desolate world that is reinforced even more by the game's Photo Mode. The graphics are beautiful and the soundtrack, sound design, and voice acting perfectly compliments the theme of the game and enhances the storytelling elements. You might actually feel the coldness while playing Frostpunk.

Performance was a bit choppy for my tastes, although it never dipped below 60FPS even during high populated cities. (i7-8700, GTX 1080, 16GB, 3840x1080). It supports ultra widescreen resolutions at 21:9 and 32:9 without any flaws. It never crashed on me as well and I didn't encounter any game breaking or any bugs at all.

[h1]Value[/h1]
Frostpunk is definitely worth every penny of its asking price with its challenging gameplay and excellent storytelling with four scenarios and an endless mode, even better if you get it on sale. Replayability only becomes an issue once you've already replayed a good chunk of the game so it's not a big deal breaker. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
If you're a fan of city building survival games, take the leap and get Frostpunk. Just don't expect hundreds of hours of sandbox gameplay content. It's more of a quality over quantity game.

[i]Frostpunk[/i] is a beautiful and haunting city builder that thinks a bit too highly of itself.

11 bit's previous creation, [i]This War of Mine[/i], was lauded not only for the gameplay (well-executed, but typical for the genre), but also for the mood and the anti-war message. And while [i]Frostpunk[/i] takes place in an even more fictional setting, with people rebuilding society after the 'global cooling', it could not resist the temptation to be a bit more that just your usual gamey-game fun.

Did it succeed? I'm not sure.

[h1]THE GOOD[/h1]
[i]Frostpunk[/i] does a lot of things right. The image of people digging a hole and trying to find warmth and comfort amidst snow is both endearing and motivating—and experience familar to everyone to at least some degree. The circular structure of the settlement is refreshing compared to traditional rectangular grids. The presentation is brilliant, with stylish art and dramatic music.

Most importantly though, while the buildings are hard to distinguish (which becomes an issue later), the developers have done a stellar job creating icons, hints, and other visual clues that help you navigate the screen. It is unavoidable for a game of this kind to become a mess of icons and numbers at some point, but [i]Frostpunk[/i] actually mostly avoids it.

The process is ever pleasant.

[h1]THE AMBIVALENT[/h1]
Call it 'streamlined' or 'shallow', but one thing is certain: [i]Frostpunk[/i] doesn't offer much in terms of strategic depth. Sure, you have two 'Purpose' ability trees to choose from (but they achieve the same goal). Sure, you can either make automatons or hoard raw manpower—but generally speaking, your progress is rather linear, spiced up with scripted events instead of robust systems.

The upside is that, due to this, the endgame is manageable and not complex to an unfun extent (as it so often gets in games about growth and development). 

The downside is clear: the game doesn't offer much in terms of replayability. It's almost story-driven.

Which brings us to...

[h1]THE UGLY[/h1]
'Yes, we survived,' the game pontificated before rolling the credits, 'BUUUHT WAS IT WORTH IT?'

It then tried to count my sins, but only came up with me employing child labor—I managed to finish the first scenario while mostly choosing humane laws and treating my people well.

And yet the game tried to lecture me. Because lecturing the player was its goal from the start. No matter which laws you ebacted. No matter if you had a different option or were just playing the game as presented to you by the developer, who chose to make it relatively dark (which [b]you[/b] for some reason are supposed to feel guilty about).

It boasts to be testing your empathy, but the people in your town are faceless units rather that characters, and you never feel any sort of attachment to them.

All in all, the moralistic part of the game fell completely flat to me.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
[i]Frostpunk[/i] claims to offer you insight into the horrors of society, but only delivers a half-hearted sermon. it's also not very replayable.

But if you disregard those points, the actual content it has to offer is really, really good and definitely worth the price tag if you're into the genre.

This is not really a colony builder. It's a RTS resource gathering race. An extinction event is coming an you need to gather enough resources to survive a chance. So what you're really doing is finding the optimal RTS build order. The colony simulation just provides the context for your race against time. 
This is really fun to begin with, but has a few problems:

* The big problem with the game is that it's easy to race ahead of the challenges once you know what you're doing. With plenty of resources none of the "hard choices" matter.
This results in each scenario having no replayability, and even the new challenges between different scenarios provides too few differences. The same build order is successful with just a few minor tweaks. 
* Another problem is that the scenarios tend to drag on. There's a lot of times you just fast forward until next building can be placed, or scouts reaches the next outpost, etc. 
* The final issue is that the game performance degrades towards the end as your population booms and graphics effects reaches the climax.

So know that is is 10-25h of entertainment (depending on how soon you're bored with the same mechanics) before you buy this. But it is at least 10h of high quality entertainment. So I think it's worth the money, but maybe get it on first sale.

This game *feels* like it has substance, but there's nothing under that admittedly-wonderful aesthetic.  They did nail the atmosphere and tension.  If those are enough for you, or if the price tag warrants a good couple of playthroughs of the first scenario, please do buy it.  Those first two playthroughs are great, because you haven't gotten past the pretty surface yet.

Once you do get underneath the veneer, though, you realize that this game with all the potential realizes none of it.  There's no room for any creativity or style.  You're stuck whittling your early build order, and there is a "correct" path and an "incorrect" path.  This isn't a Civilization-type game where you can develop tech and law your own way, feeling it out and reacting as necessary.  This game is more Starcraft, where you have to nail the exact timing and order of one of a very few predetermined paths based on scripted events.  In fact, if you do well early on in the scenario, you'll be penalized heavily for not *waiting* to do well until after a scripted event: now you've blown all your Hope laws and the event robbed you of all hope.  Similarly, if you're on endurance mode, you'd better have those child-supported infirmaries up before the first storm, even if it means sacrificing everything else.  Your priorities are not your own.

Sorry, devs, I can see a lot of love was put into that atmosphere, but in the end, that's all the game has: atmosphere, tension, and about 6 hours of discovery.

Bottom line is that Frostpunk is a puzzle game, not a strategy / management / city builder game, so those looking for the latter will likely be disappointed (and won't realize it during the refund period, to boot).

First, I want to address the notion that this game is "difficult". Sure, most if not all players will have a high rate of failure on initial scenario playthroughs, but this is not due to "difficulty"; rather, it's due to each scenario's differing emphasis on certain resources, along with multiple scripted new objectives that occur over the course of the scenario, both of which are initially unknown to the player. Once the player knows what the emphases and objectives are - and they play out the same way every time - the player knows what build order is necessary to get around these obstacles, including build timings that only make sense in the context of knowing what's coming next. Hence, puzzle game.

A further problem is that the gameplay path to avoid outright failure is so narrow that there is a clear best path to actions and choices throughout a scenario. So it is not only merely a matter of figuring out this optimal progression, but it's a waste of time to try to figure out different or novel ways to approach the scenarios - and this kills the replayability. Again, it's a puzzle game.

It's a shame as I really like the environment they've created. It's wonderfully immersive, there's a very consistent look and feel (and even dare I say emotion) to the game, heck I even loved the surround sound which is something I'd never thought I'd care about in this genre. The UI is really good and the game runs fantastic. But ultimately this game fails where it matters; there's just no depth and there's no strategy / management / city building to it.

TLDR: it's quite entertaining, and worth a go for the right price. But the obvious DLC trojan horse mars what is quite a short game with not a huge amount of depth.

This is another one of those games I really struggle to thumbs up or down. But the fundamental reasons I voted down are twofold. One is that the game interface - despite me buying the base game - has many options I can't use. It lists five levels, but you realise actually those last two don't exist. Three's a freeform mode with three options, but then you realise that much of that is unavailable.

And that annoys me. I bought a game. Sell DLC - fine. I am fine with that. But don't put all these dead ends in the product I bought. Don't rub my nose in the content I don't own, blending it with my game so I don't know what I do own. It adds to annoyance and it's disrespectful.

And indeed a lot of the marketing of this game and the DLC makes it hard to properly understand what you are getting.

The other issue is you then realise you have effectively three proper campaign modes. Three. That's it. That's quite poor. Yes the freeform mode adds a bit more, but it's rather lacking in a point.  And again, you will end up finding so much content is locked.

Three levels I passed, and was dumped at the menu each time after a short (admittedly lovely) cut scene. There's nothing stitching these missions together at all. No consequences. For all the world building, there's no narrative that pulls it together. 

The game itself is quite enjoyable. It is a game where you have to learn what it wants, and do it. This game does not value ingenuity. When the game says you need to get 7500k coal in two days... well you aren't going to do that. You need to start again and reevaluate your decisions.

And it is rather enjoyable going back, re-thinking, learning to adapt. Normally I'm a turtler. Normally I like freeform modes. This game forced me to to think and adapt and act FAST. That's where the game works well.

But sadly when you peel back, it's not that in-depth. You are forced to largely play the way the game wants you to.  You won't build a hospital proactively, because you soon learn that if you wait for the game to ask you and *then* do it you'll get a bonus for doing so. 

The tech tree is quite basic and is the same across all missions. Once you work out that formula there is a sense of you know it and can repeat it. Some of the tough decisions you have to make - for example do you let sick people die in the cold - don't really have a massive impact at the end of the day. It'd be great if you had a sense of decisions REALLY having an impact. Like so many board games are legacy games now, where is the legacy of what you do here? The game doesn't really care.

It's not terrible by any means. It's quite fun. But only get it if the price is under the £10 mark, and be prepared to hit lots of walls as the DLC monster locks you out of the game you bought.

I take pride in the little things - unlike other cities, our children don't labour in the camps with the other workers. The storm is coming - as I continuously punish citizens for stealing food supplies or not doing their fair part in labour, I urge them to keep pressing on for the ultimate goal - our survival depends on cooperation and hoarding of precious coal and food. Frostpunk is a steampunk post-apocalyptic 'survival city builder' - one where you become hopelessly invested in the wellbeing of a virtually faceless population, and every sentence ends with 'and then things got worse'.

Things are already pretty bad when you begin the main story; the unexplained climate and societal collapse causes refugees to flee, Fallout Vault style, to isolated generators which pump up heat from the earth to shelter small communities from the snow. As you might suspect, it's pretty stressful being one of a handful of people just trying to stay alive in deeply sub-zero temperatures... but then It Gets Worse. As days go by, the temperature will drop more and more precipitously - avoiding spoilers, you (the player-manager of New London) will need to gather resources, research improvements, and sign laws in order to keep your population not only alive, but also contented and hopeful. Naturally, therefore, the challenge comes from balancing all of these as Things Get Worse for the settlers.

There's a lot to say about the game mechanics - which I would usually put here, but will instead leave further down so that potential new players can experience the game as naively as possible. What must be made clear, however, is how incredibly invested you become in your communities, and how (surprisingly) emotionally taxing it can be when they crumble. I have never cried at a movie and generally don't get hit by strong bursts of emotion, but it was hard not to get a little choked up during the final cutscene, after you've experienced first-hand the struggles settlers have gone through and the decisions you feel you had to make which have lead to, perhaps, more pain and suffering that they need've experienced. The same goes for each of the DLC scenarios, which I experienced several years after completing the main storyline - the [spoiler]failure of a healthcare system overwhelmed by refugees, with each death toll a stab in the heart[/spoiler] in The Refugees; [spoiler]explosion of the generator before you've managed to evacuate everyone[/spoiler] in The Fall of Winterhome; the [spoiler]coming of the first frost, or the industrial accidents[/spoiler] in The Last Autumn; the [spoiler]desperate gathering of supplies for a New London on the brink of collapse[/spoiler] in On The Edge - each one brought those same emotional highs and lows. [strike]I will go into more detail about the DLCs when I review the Season Pass specifically, but[/strike] can't do that lol. To summarise: each scenario functions like a total conversion mod of the main game - some, like The Last Autumn, are virtually unrecognisable at the beginning - but each is, undeniably, worth your time after the main story.

I played Frostpunk back when it first came out, and (at the time, on a different website) wrote something about the morality system at play, on which the real, player-imposed 'challenge' is based on. In short: when it came out - and, I believe, to this day - it contained one of the more thoughtful approaches to video game morality i'd seen up to that point, an enormous leap forward from Bioshock-tier 'press x to be a terrible person' mechanics. The game forces you to choose between two ideological systems (based on either 'order' or 'faith') which, on top of the positive effects on hope and discontent, provide production and health/healing bonuses respectively; this starts off pretty innocuously with watchtowers and chapels, but as you enact laws deeper into that tech tree it rapidly escalates into propaganda centres and crucifixions. Crucially, however, the extent to which the player-manager delves into the thinly-veiled communist or theocratic nightmare is, ultimately, up to them; when I watched streamers play it at the time, this caused a certain amount of anger as many of them believed they were 'forced' into extreme measures, and adopted an interesting denialism that it could have gone any different - which can be disproven almost immediately on a second playthrough, since understanding of the game mechanics and the general progression of the game makes it quite easy to keep things cheerful, with no need to resort to public executions, torture, etc. That's not to say it's a loss-condition as such to descend into hell, except for insofar as you feel quite bad about torturing a bunch of people; the game will [spoiler]admonish you during the final cutscene if you have 'gone too far'[/spoiler], but will [spoiler]praise you if you don't. 'The line', in case you were wondering, is protector of the truth/righteous denunciation and pledge of loyalty/forceful persuasion - mostly reasonable, I think, although one which has the potential to cause arguments and fuel denialism[/spoiler]. It is this self-reflection - on top of the normal 'discontent was too high/hope was too low' - which constitutes the real challenge, and it's one pulled off so well that you, like me, might well be mulling it over for a while after you've uninstalled the game.

[i]Spoilers end.[/i]

For a compelling story told almost entirely through textboxes, a harrowing struggle against mounting odds, and a thoughtful, reflective attitude to in-game morality, Frostpunk was my singleplayer game of 2018, if not the decade, and remains one of my 'must-plays'. Buy it, play it, consider how fragile life is and the lies we tell ourselves when we shatter it.

[h1]The City Must Survive[/h1]

The first time I played Frostpunk was in the winter of 2019. I was snowed in at my Chicago apartment and was rather unsuccessfully attempting to get over an exceptionally irksome head cold. If you are perusing the store page and happen upon the game’s promotional material, you will understand why it caught my eye in this particular moment. It was as good a time as any to boot it up. After all, if you’re the kind who organizes games by season, Frostpunk is unquestionably a winter game. And a great one, at that.

Additionally, the game comes with a solid pedigree. Aside from being so heavily rooted in its genre, it is also an extension (of sorts) of 11 Bit Studios’ work on This War of Mine. While the games are undeniably dissimilar as far as gameplay and story beats, they still feature numerous mechanical parallels. And the same mood. And the same sadness. And the same desperation. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2361711665 

It is obvious that 11 Bit Studios is interested in how people adapt when pressed to the limit, as they now have two successive titles that push this concept. The main difference between the two games, other than that of category, lies within the narrative itself. This War of Mine was about the survival of the individual; Frostpunk is about the survival of the collective. Both leave it up to the player to wager the worth of either.

In the past, [i]you[/i] must survive. Here, [i]the city[/i] must survive.

[h1]Heavy Lies the Crown[/h1]
Frostpunk combines city management systems and real-time strategy with familiar survival game elements. The player represents the head of a community set in the post-apocalyptic frozen wasteland of the British Isles. The rabble you are leading is originally from London, which is fitting, as the entirety of the aesthetic of Frostpunk is almost assuredly late-Victorian era and, of course, steampunk. 

As the leader in this frozen wasteland, your goal is to provide the people with their essential needs: food, shelter, and warmth. Investing too heavily in trying to secure one will risk imperiling the populace with lack of another. So, the key becomes managing them efficiently. 

But priorities shift rapidly, as do temperatures, which make it nearly impossible to stay on top of all your tasks simultaneously. Which, oddly, is kind of a good thing…

One of the main issues that 11 Bit Studios had with This War of Mine was that if the player became too proficient, the game became duller. Mistakes allowed for your situation to become more desperate. More desperate was more fun. Pathos still existed when you played well, but the entire endeavor seemed to forget that the primary focus of a video game should always be to entertain the player—not just lecture to them.  And if you were really good at This War of Mine, and things were going very well, it was relatively easy for the game to become stagnant.

This is not the case in Frostpunk.

[h1]Our Shepherd Leads Us. But to What End?[/h1]
The city will be fine. The populace will be working. The resources will be overflowing. And the weather will be mild. But then the temperature will plummet. It will be too cold to hunt. People will get ill. The coal mines will deplete. And hope will be lost.

Frostpunk is a story about how things fall apart.

In my three playthroughs of the game, I was never able to completely master its complexities. The game is almost exclusively geared toward making the entire endeavor feel completely insurmountable. It is not a game for people who are afraid to lose. It doesn’t care to be, either. The game’s mechanics, aided by incredible aesthetics and music, desire to make the player feel one thing—hopeless. That is the long and short of it. And it works. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2361710920 

Moral dilemmas are ubiquitous.

The people will come to you, begging for more bread. Or to go back to London, where they came from. Or for a day off work. Or anything. And you will have to choose. Do you value the individual or the collective? Whose needs require immediate attention?  What do you do when you have barely enough food to feed your own people and then refugees show up at your gates? What do you do when you don’t have enough coal to keep the heat running and your only choice is to enforce a 24-hour workday in a deadly mine? 

Or when you don’t have enough food, shelter, and warmth, how long before you send the children to work in that same mine? 

Frostpunk is not interested in moral posturing, as these life-or-death decisions eventually come too frequently and usually without much warning. You simply have too much responsibility and too many emergent peripheral items to really contemplate each verdict. And the very fact that the demands of your doomed people become background noise compared to the daily concerns that you, the player, carry underscores the game’s thesis: people will do what they need to do.

The city must survive; your soul, well…

[h1]The Darkest of Days[/h1]
Most city or park simulation games feature an inherent detachment from the player and the people. Or rather, it is almost always kept at a superficial level. As an example, when you build a new roller coaster in a theme park simulation, you are typically going to get general, cursory feedback from the people who ride the roller coaster. The results are usually binary. The player either built a good roller coaster or they did not. 

Frostpunk isn’t remotely like that.

Your people feel like actual characters rather than generic models or numbers. Mostly because every choice the leader makes normally receives flavored reactions catered to specifically address that selection. If you enforce a new law that is unpopular, you will hear about it—and you will have to deal with all consequences of that action. And because there is almost always a [i]good[/i] reason to enact a [i]bad[/i] policy, binary results are more difficult to detect. Yes, I may be morally corrupt for printing manipulative propaganda to get my people to go to work, but if they are more likely to go to work because of it, then we are all more likely to survive. 

It’s for their own good, you see. Right? 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2361712008 

The story of your city begins to manifest through every one of your decisions and its consequences. When it all fails, it is easy to see who is to blame. You will carry the burden. Which is exactly how it should be. 

This is an excellent design. 

As mentioned, this game is not for people who fear failure. Because you will fail. The player will sooner or later be made to understand the impossible breadth of their task. Once you sense that everything you built will soon come crumbling down, that is when Frostpunk achieves the full authenticity it sought. It simply would not work as an easy game. 

Surviving this cruel winter is great, but nothing quite equals the absolute terror when, at 100 below zero, your heat source shuts down because you’ve mismanaged your coal. 

And now everyone is going to die.

It’s absolutely thrilling.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Frostpunk is a mechanically sound city-sim focused on survival. The player is tasked with creating a metropolis focused solely on the ability of its people to overcome an apocalyptic winter. 

It is an easy game to lose. And that is okay. The game relies on the player’s desperation in order to appropriately sell its themes. And, naturally, the player would appreciate a positive outcome more if it took the necessary fortitude to achieve that end.

Bundle up. Eat light. Work hard. 

The city must survive.

…but can it?

I got this game once for free on epic, but solely the base game. After I played a bit the main scenario, I immediately bought it on steam as I wanted more of the game, and I don’t buy any games on epic.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
The idea is that you build a small city around a giant machine while managing heat and other resources. There are 4 Scenarios being usually around 2-4 hours in play time. They each have some unique twist to them. As an example, in one you have to horde masses amount of food and prepare houses as a slowly bigger storm of refugees arrive in a wave. In another one you have mostly to keep up the heat of seed vaults.
Buildings that are closer to the machine usually don’t need heating on their own so its good to build houses or medical stations there while buildings that are warm anyways  like workshops for research can be placed further away. 

Additionally from building heat sources, deciding which building to research next or build, you can have scouts that traverse a non-random map with resources, stories and other stuff to find. The difficulty in the game is usually with the scenarios main goal and additionally the heat will drop and rise but slowly being lower than before meaning old buildings may not retain liveable condition and needs to be heated or people will get sick or die.

There are also some political rules/choices you can make which can go into a fascist dictatorship or religious rule. Generally, the religious path is just way superior because they have better bonuses and do not require men all time to patrol the streets.

The game is played in a way that you barely can win on the normal difficulty if you don’t know what’s coming. As some have scripted scenarios that can lose your game if you didn’t quick save all time.  For me it was incredibly fun to try and build different approaches managing to finally beat a map and I feel like for that the main “normal” difficulty is a good challenge between not too hard and not too easy if you accept that you might need to retry once or twice. The higher difficulties on the other hand don’t feel that fun as they are feeling like a lot RNG based and on top of that you basically have to follow 1: 1 guide to beat them.
Overall if you beat everything you can also do an endless mode but for that the game wasn’t really programmed or at least mainly intended and balanced. Beating the scenarios is incredibly fun but its rather short lived as without DLC there are only 4 which u beat probably in around 10 hours. After that you can do miscellaneous achievements in case you want to continue playing but I found the game had way too many and some being repetitive like play a run without building a or building b etc. Or misleading ones as there are no death achievements despite the game featuring scripted deaths anyways.

[u]Story[/u]
I found the scenarios stories fun and engaging having various sudden plot twists and while also giving some smaller decisions. Overall really engaging and immersive having also some smaller lore info’s sprinkled into the loading screen as there are wide arrange of contrary opinions about the cold or they explain the reason why the game is even set at the artic.

[u]Sound[/u]
The game features heavily violins and generally orchestra music which also ends into a very heavy cascade in the finale of a scenario making the city must survive one of the best songs I have ever heard in any video game.
Also the general sound design is conveying the danger and threat of the barely habitable surroundings perfectly from its heavy on duty warning noises, to snow storms pillaging across the area.

[u]Graphics[/u]
Im always impressed with these base buildings games animation of diverse buildings and characters. Its fun to look around and see what kind of building does what. This doesn’t feature this a lot and is more focused on A LOT of images that have small animations adding its own style to them. This type of animation style always looks fantastic and is in the game almost everywhere to be seen and rarely these repeat.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
I found the game very engaging due to its unique setting, great orchestra OST and fun gameplay that while not being too complex still is something rather unique with its heat management system. There are sadly only a few scenarios but those that exist are really good, wanting me to tackle them on higher difficulties albeit I found the higher difficulties more frustrating than fun. The endless mode isn’t really balanced that great and therefore my biggest critique is the rather short gameplay time. And me saying I want more of the game is more or less a good thing.

Frostpunk is a post apocalyptic city builder from 11 Bit Studios, the developers of This War of Mine and the Anomaly series. Set in the late 19th century, the world has been devastated by a new ice age, and the player is in charge of a group of civilians who have left London in the hope of establishing a new settlement around a massive heat generator.

You'll need to gather four types of resources - coal to power the generator, wood and steel to construct buildings and research upgrades, and of course your citizens will need food. The temperature starts at -20C and quickly becomes much colder, so you'll need to upgrade the generator's power, and as you start to build further away from the generator, you'll need to upgrade its range. When people are cold they'll get sick, and eventually die if left untreated, so you'll need to build warm houses and medical facilities. You can send scouts outside the city in search of supplies and other survivors. 

You’ll often be in a situation where you don’t have enough workers to assign to every task, especially in the early game, so you need to decide what the most important priorities are. Maybe you should take engineers off research to help deal with a medical crisis, or perhaps you should reassign some hunters because your coal reserves are running low. This can become more difficult when civilians working in freezing conditions suffer frostbite, potentially requiring life saving amputations, leaving them unable to work until you can manufacture prosthetic limbs in a factory. After a while you can unlock the ability to construct automatons – giant machines which can replace entire teams of workers, will work overnight without complaining, and are immune to the cold.
 
Similar to This War of Mine, Frostpunk has a bleak atmosphere where it feels like survival is a constant struggle, and the game often asks the player to make difficult decisions which you might think are in the best interest of the city, but are likely to make your citizens unhappy. For example, you could increase your available workforce by approving the use of child labour. Or you could respond to a shortage of a particular resource by ordering the related production buildings to work 24 hour shifts. You can improve happiness with entertainment buildings like the tavern or fighting arena, but if happiness falls too low, your people will kick you out of the city, resulting in game over. Part way through the story you'll have to decide whether to focus on order or religion, to keep the peace and prevent crime, and this choice allows access to different buildings and laws.
 
Its a tough learning curve, and while a successful campaign in the story mode should only take around 7-8 hours to complete, you might not succeed on your first attempt. My first city failed around day 31, but honestly I'd been stumbling from one crisis to the next for the whole game. But I learned enough that my second city was far more efficient, and I was better prepared for things to go wrong. The endgame was still brutal though, and pushed me right to the limit. And since the game originally released, the developers have added 3 extra scenarios which add several more hours of gameplay. They aren’t just more of the same on a different map, as they feature unique objectives that will affect your playing style, as well as adding more details to the story.

They’ve also added an endless mode, but unfortunately my playthrough is crashing at the exact same moment (7am, day 16) every time I attempt to progress, which appears to have ended my time with the game on a disappointing note.
 
Frostpunk is an excellent game that I strongly recommend everyone to check out, although it might be best to wait for some more patches, or a discount.

This has been one of my favorite games of all time. When you first play, you're met with devastation and impossible choices. They become easier as you, the steward, must do what is needed, not what is best, for your people. It has brought endless hours of frustration and hope. 
The only thing I regret is that they pivoted to Frostpunk 2 instead of providing more DLC and expansions for the original. I am not a big fan of City Sims over all and have not played many. 
However, I do love steampunk and such things, that is why I chose to give Frostpunk a try. 

If you DO like steampunk and/or other similar things as well as Sims, this is the game for you. 

And I love it. The style of the game, the various missions with varied objectives and some tweaked restrictions and options makes it a whole lot of fun. The game offers large variation in how hard you want to make the game to be, from the initial difficulty level to the in-game choices you want to make. 
The non-square building-map layout and area of affects that buildings have give a new and more interesting twist to trying and build as a efficient society as possible. 
The cinematics/cutscenes are super good, the style suits the game perfectly and the it gives the game a really fitting atmoshphere. The voiceover is also amazing! 

There are however a few things that I think are annoying. Not necessarily bad tho. 
1, Some mechanics(?) are a bit clunky and that makes it hard to effectivly manage a larger city. 
2, Sometimes it feels like there should be more choice in what you are able to do when it comes to policy. Especially since the secondary choice of policy tree is quite shallow but gives very large effects. 

Finally, this is not really a complaint, but something I wish for: More content
The game is not bad as I have said above and does not lack replay-capability, but I am a guy who loves grinding missions. The 3 optional scenarios are good, but after you have beaten them twice or so, it makes it less challenging. You also want to explore more of the worl and the game: "What happened", "What will happen after The Great Winter?", "Are any of the societies you build sustainable?" Etc. Shortly put, I WANT MORE OF THIS GAME! :) They did provided an update with endless-mode which is a good start, but after you have maxed out the tech tree you can pretty much set it on auto-pilot, which is not really fun. 

I hope this review helped some of you who read it! 
Good luck and wrap up well, the cold is here!

Frostpunk is a brutal, yet incredibly immersive city-builder where every decision feels heavy. Balancing the survival of your people with tough moral choices is both stressful and rewarding. This isn't really a city builder — it's a series of impossible choices dressed up as one. Every law you pass, every resource you ration, every worker you push past their limit chips away at something, and the game never lets you forget it. There's no clean way to win. You just decide what you're willing to live with.

The generator hum, the constant temperature readout, the way the whole map just fades into white the further you look — the atmosphere alone does more storytelling than most games manage with actual dialogue. And when the storms hit, genuine panic sets in. Not "oh no, a setback" panic. Real, gut-level "we might not make it" panic.

Book of Laws is where the game really shows its teeth. Child labor. Public executions. Forced overtime. Nothing is presented as good or evil, just necessary or not, and that ambiguity is what makes it stick with you long after you've closed the game.

Bleak, brutal, brilliant. Not a comfortable game, but an unforgettable one.

I'll admit I walked in to the game knowing it from top till' bottom. Which undoubtedly, spoiled my experience. Keep that in mind as you read this.

In about mid-game you get one of two choices. They're both different skins of the same thing. They offer nothing different at all, except ascetics. 

The main story can be completed in less than an hour if you know what you're doing and playing on full speed. (This got a lot of people angry so let me elaborate.)
A day on full speed is exactly one minute. It's roughly 40 days long. (It can vary a few days) Add some minutes for scouting, building and you're looking at close to or little more than an hour.

My first playthrough was about 3 hours and 30 minutes.
If you're going in blind I'd guess you'd be looking at something more like 6 hours to complete the main story. Unless you turn it down to easy. Then it's a cakewalk.

There is no endless mode. I can see why. There is quite literally nothing to do once you've become self sufficient. So in this sense I'm happy they decided to have a story with a proper ending.
The story itself is very simple and sadly isn't explored as much as I'd like. You'll have almost as many questions walking out as you did walking in.

There are two extra scenarios that could have justified the buy if they were of the same quality and length as the main story. Unfortunately they both seem very hastily thrown together just to offer something more than the short main story.

Despite the cons the game itself is very good. What it does I have no problems with at all. It's a refreshing game that I'd honestly recommend to people who haven't seen anything of it. I think your experience would be 10 times better if you went in blind unlike me.

I don't think anyone playing this will think it's a bad game. I just think people might end up feeling disappointed by the short lifespan of it all.

Final words: A good game that does pretty much everything right gameplay wise, but severely lacks length and reasons to replay the few scenarios that are there.

Gameplay lasts about 4-8 hours for the main campaign, and you will have seen everything the game has to offer long before then. The developers promised a game about societal evolution, but the main campaign automatically ends between day 45 and 50. The other scenarios are even shorter and last 10-20 days. I beat the main campaign on my first attempt and there is absolutely no replay value to be had. No sandbox. No survival mode. No random scenarios. Just 1 linear campaign for 45 days and two afterthought scenarios that will give a few additional hours of gameplay. You will have the opportunity to select all or nearly all laws on both trees. Whichever optional tree you choose, they essentially do the same thing: prevent societal unrest (though with different colored bars).  There are about 10 laws per tree and most of them are uninteresting (hope +/-X, discontent +/-X without any real change to gameplay). 

The tech tree is terribly uninspired, consisting mostly of +X% to this resource or a "new" building that gives +X% to a resource.

Exploration? Essentially, it's click to get +X resources with a chance of some people dying. Or choose between getting more survivors or letting them die. That's it: no moral choice, no real strategic choice.  The exploration sites are all static and do not offer any replay value.

The few "moral choice" cutscenes/events are rendered meaningless by the fact that there are no named characters, very little in the way of recurring or multi-part events and simply no real gameplay impact. You'll be given 2-3 options to choose from. Each one will raise or lower hope/discontent in various combinations. Again, no meaningful impact beyond the two bars on your screen. 

On top of the glaring lack of content, there are several quality of life issues like being unable to see a map of what building types you have or set building abilities to automatic use (resulting in a tedious process of selecting and clicking the same abilities on the same buildings every few minutes). 

This game is not even close to being worth the asking price. The developers, coasting on the success of their previous title This War of Mine, dramatically overpromised and underdelivered. Frostpunk almost froze me out before it won me over.

I finished the main scenario, A New Home, on Normal difficulty in 11h across roughly ten attempts. That number says a lot about my experience. At first, I was close to dropping the game and giving it a 3/10.

The biggest problem is the learning curve. There is a lot to manage. Food, wood, coal, steel, heat, illness, workforce, hope and discontent all demand attention at once.

The early game is also the most important part of a run. You need to make crucial decisions before you fully understand their consequences, and recovering from a bad opening feels extremely difficult. Most of the time, restarting seemed more practical than trying to save a city that had already fallen behind.

Once the game clicked, though, my opinion changed completely.

The gameplay has a great sense of progression. The first week requires constant micromanagement, with every worker and resource feeling important. Later, the city becomes more stable and you finally have space to plan instead of constantly reacting.

Then the final stretch turns everything into survival panic. Without spoiling anything, Frostpunk does an excellent job of making you prepare for something terrible while never letting you feel completely ready. You start questioning every decision, every stockpile and every building you constructed.

It goes from stressful to memorable, and the ending was easily one of the strongest parts of the game.

The atmosphere is excellent. This is not just a city-builder about placing structures efficiently around a generator. The people feel like actual survivors, even without traditional named characters.

The graphics sell the cold incredibly well. Watching the city disappear beneath the snow creates a real sense of isolation and claustrophobia. The circular building system around the generator also makes the city visually satisfying to organize, which naturally meant mine had to be as neat as possible.

Scouting and outposts add more planning outside the city, while the law system gives Frostpunk its moral weight. You can introduce policies involving child labor, overcrowded hospitals, alcohol and the treatment of the dead. Most choices provide a practical benefit, but often at an uncomfortable human cost.

That tension is what makes Frostpunk more than a normal city-builder. It is not only asking whether your city is efficient. It is asking what kind of society you are willing to create when survival becomes the only priority.

My experience was a complete turnaround. The opening is confusing, unforgiving and too dependent on knowledge gained through failure. I still think the game should teach its systems better and allow more room to recover from early mistakes.

But once it clicks, the city-building is satisfying, the atmosphere is fantastic and the moral choices feel meaningful.

In the end, you can have all the resources in the world. You will still need a little faith. A little hope that your decisions were enough, that the city will survive and that everything will somehow be all right.

TL;DR: Frostpunk gave me a terrible first impression, with a harsh learning curve and an early game that feels very difficult to recover from when things go wrong. Once I understood its systems, however, it became a tense, atmospheric and surprisingly emotional city-builder where every resource and moral decision matters. 8/10.
